Built ElasticSeer for the Elastic AgentBuilder Hackathon, an autonomous incident response system that detects anomalies in Elasticsearch, correlates logs/traces with Gemini 2.5 Flash + MCP, and automatically opens a GitHub PR, alerts Slack, and creates a Jira ticket. The goal was to reduce the manual workload that usually comes with sudden incidents. Stack: Elasticsearch Serverless, ES|QL, Elastic Workflows, Gemini 2.5 Flash, MCP. And Elastic was especially useful here because the ES|QL + observability stack made it easy to correlate logs, traces, and anomalies in real time without a lot of extra infrastructure. Last week, I went to the ArmyXTech Hackathon. Our team built Hawk-I — a real-time C2 platform focused on protecting logistics in contested environments. The idea was to connect cyber events and real-world supply chain impact using the AIP Ontology. We ingested OSINT sources (FlightRadar, AIS shipping, Exa AI, Kaggle datasets) alongside cyber telemetry from Shodan to map how disruptions like grid outages or infrastructure attacks affect frontline operations. We also built a RAG-based decision support agent that generates Courses of Action (COAs) with full lineage and human verification through Foundry. Due to foundry limitations as well, we had to use Notional data sourced from real events. Check out the project here: https://lnkd.in/gNb_ga6Q Thanks Shield Capital and Cerebral Valley for this experience. #SupplyChain #AI #HawkI #Hackathon #Palantir #CerebralValley #DefenseTech #NationalSecurity #BuildInPublic ...more

A reactor in the Utah desert powered an Nvidia chip. Weeks later, Sequoia wired $1 billion. ⚛️ Valar Atomics is three years old. The round values it at $6 billion, triple its April mark. A $200 million credit facility takes the total to $1.2 billion. What earned it: → Ward 250, their helium-cooled reactor, went critical on 18 June → First reactor to do that outside a national laboratory → Its electricity then ran an Nvidia Blackwell system in a live demo → Valar & Nvidia are planning a 30 MW nuclear-powered AI facility in Utah The thesis is not "build a better reactor." It is "stop building reactors like construction projects and start manufacturing them like products." One reactor is a project. A fleet is a production line. The hard part is ahead. Valar still needs an NRC licence before it sells a single watt. But AI data centres are pulling more power than grids can hand over. Energy is the real bottleneck in AI. Congrats Isaiah Taylor and the team. 👏

We applied to 4 accelerators: Y Combinator, 500 Global, Plug and Play, and Berkeley SkyDeck. Before that I went through 30+ programs worldwide. For roughly the same 12 weeks, you can pay 0% equity or 12%. Almost nobody compares them properly. Here are the 10 worth a founder's time. 1. Y Combinator (SF Bay Area) $125K for 7%, plus $375K on an uncapped MFN SAFE. No fees. 3 months. Outcome: Demo Day in front of the most active seed investors alive. The brand reprices your round. 2. a16z Speedrun (San Francisco) $500K for 10%, plus $500K in your next round within 18 months. $8M+ in credits, no board seat. 12 weeks, 60-70 teams, twice a year. Outcome: a16z as your first investor. 3. HF0 (San Francisco) Reported at $1M for 5%. 12 weeks, live-in. Outcome: ~10 teams per cohort, mostly repeat founders. Best terms on this list if you get in. 4. South Park Commons (SF, NYC, Bangalore) $400K for 7% now, plus $600K guaranteed at your next round. 8-week bootcamp, then open-ended residency. Outcome: built for the -1 to 0 stage, before you know what you're building. 5. Sequoia Arc (Americas and Europe) A 4-day intensive, ~10 companies. Terms are company-specific and not published. Outcome: Sequoia partners engaged pre-seed. Shortest program here by a wide margin. 6. Techstars (30+ cities worldwide) $220K: $20K for 5% common, plus $200K uncapped MFN SAFE. No fee. 3 months. APAC programs run $100K instead. Outcome: mentor-driven, but quality varies enormously by city. Pick the MD, not the logo. 7. 500 Global (Global) $150K for ~6% (negotiable). 4 months. Outcome: the most distribution-focused curriculum of the large programs. 2,500+ companies backed. 8. Entrepreneur First (London, San Francisco, Bangalore) Equity-free grant while you're still ideating, then up to $250K once you incorporate. Equity not published. Outcome: they back you before you have a co-founder or an idea. Nobody else does this at scale. 9. Berkeley SkyDeck (Berkeley, plus a Milan track) $200K for 7.5%. 6 months. 20-25 teams per batch. Outcome: strong Demo Day plus Berkeley's talent pipeline. Catch: one founder must be UC-affiliated or an international founder. 10. Plug and Play (Global) The program is equity-free. Investment is separate and optional. Outcome: Fortune 500 pilots, not investor intros. 80+ vertical programs a year. Also strong: Antler (30 cities, terms vary), EWOR (up to €500K, Europe), Alchemist (enterprise). Equity turns out to be the wrong thing to optimize. Plug and Play takes 0% and gets you corporate pilots. YC takes 7% and gets you a seed round at several times the price you'd raise alone. Both are right, for different companies. We went with YC, 500 Global, Plug and Play and Berkeley SkyDeck. Which ones would you have applied to in our position? Genuinely asking.

I think one of the biggest limitations of today’s AI is that its assumptions about how work gets done are already outdated. Ask it to plan a project and it’ll often estimate six months because that’s what software development looked like in the world it learned from. The problem isn’t the timeline. It’s that every recommendation that follows is conditioned on that assumption. What should you build? Which architecture should you choose? What should you prioritize? Those decisions all depend on how expensive the model believes software development is. Simply retraining on newer data probably won’t fully solve this. Training data teaches models how work was done, not how work changes when AI is doing a significant fraction of it. I think future AI systems will need to continuously update their priors as AI changes the nature of work itself. Otherwise they’ll keep optimizing for constraints that no longer exist.

There is a short clip doing the rounds from Jeff Bezos that genuinely stayed with me. It comes from Tim Dodd’s exclusive tour of Blue Origin’s New Glenn factory in Cape Canaveral, Florida. What stood out was not the scale of the rocket. Bezos walks through the facility, closely observing how teams work on New Glenn. He points out details most leaders would skip. The GS1 booster’s aft section with seven BE-4 engines. The midsection tanks. The forward section. The second-stage hydrogen tank. But the real moment is his interaction with employees. He listens. He asks questions. He looks genuinely curious, not performative. I strongly resonate with this. Because leadership is not about walking the floor to be seen. It is about walking the floor to understand. The best leaders I have learned from share one habit. They stay close to the work. Not to micromanage. But to respect the people doing it. When leaders understand the details, teams feel valued. When teams feel valued, quality improves. And when quality improves, speed and innovation follow naturally. This clip is a reminder. Vision matters. But presence matters more. #leadership #amazon #workculture #jeffbezos

Today, I am excited to share that Bunkerhill Health has raised $55 million from Vinod Khosla at Khosla Ventures , Alfred Lin from Sequoia Capital , Y Combinator , and other amazing investors. Over the past year, we have partnered with more than a dozen health systems and grown revenue 20x. Today, I’m also excited to formally share what we’ve been building. Our mission is to make it radically easy for health systems to turn their ideas into reality through AI agents—improving patient outcomes, bending the cost curve, and making healthcare operations dramatically more efficient. The University of Texas Medical Branch is running 20+ AI agents - live - across the enterprise on Bunkerhill. One of those agents - in its first month - flagged a patient at imminent risk of heart attack, leading to a life-saving open heart surgery. Another one, a nephrology triage agent, cut wait times for appointments by >50%. Yet another one, a lung nodule agent, addressed urgent cases 80% faster and doubled guideline-concordant follow-ups. That is what Peter McCaffrey, MD, calls Bunkerhill: “a shared brain” for the health system. That’s the promise of AI finally being realized in healthcare. Making it possible requires two things: (1) a shared layer of intelligence for the entire health system, and (2) an operating model to enable rapid development of AI agents for the problems they understand best. Together, these dramatically reduce the cost and time required to turn an idea into a working solution. As that cost approaches zero, the limiting factor is no longer technology. It is imagination—and the conviction to act. The health systems we work with have both. Our job is to make sure nothing else stands in their way.

Traditional travel apps give you lists and ratings, but they lack the conversational warmth and immediate context of a real guide. Inspired by the desire to make exploring new cities more immersive and accessible, we built CharlieTourGuy—an AI persona that can walk you through the streets, tell you the history of a building you're looking at, and chat with you in real-time.
